title: Matthew 12:9–14
context: Continuing the Sabbath controversy (12:1–8), Jesus enters the synagogue, faces a trap question over a man with a withered hand, answers with mercy’s logic, heals, and draws the Pharisees into a plot to destroy Him.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 12:9–14, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: A man which had his hand withered - Probably through a partial paralysis. The man's hand was withered; but God's mercy had still preserved to him the use of his feet: He uses them to bring him to the public worship of God, and Jesus meets and heals him there.
arminian.source: Commentary on the New Testament (on Matt 12:9–14)

reformed.quote: This narrative and that which immediately precedes it have the same object; which is to show, that the scribes watched with a malicious eye for the purpose of turning into slander every thing that Christ did, and consequently that we need not wonder if men, whose minds were so depraved, were his implacable enemies. We see also, that it is usual with hypocrites to pursue what is nothing more than a shadow of the righteousness of the Law, and as the common saying is, to stickle more about the form than about the substance.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 12:9–14)

verses.text: He departed from there and went into their synagogue.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus does not retreat after the grainfield clash; He enters “their” synagogue—the place of worship where His critics hold influence. Presence itself is pastoral courage.

Arminian interpreters notice the pattern of grace that keeps coming near: the Lord who claims the Sabbath also walks into contested space. Hearers are summoned to meet Him where Scripture is read, not only where comfort is easy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew’s “from there” ties synagogue to the lordship claim just made. The Son of Man does not leave Sabbath theology in the field; He brings it into Israel’s gathered life.

Reformed reading hears providence and mission: Christ advances into the assembly God has ordered. The controversy that follows is not accidental; it unfolds under the Lord’s purposeful steps.

verses.text: And behold, there was a man with a withered hand. They asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day?” so that they might accuse him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Need sits in plain sight—a withered hand—yet the question is prosecution, not pity. “Is it lawful?” is aimed to accuse, not to learn. Mercy is already being weighed against a trap.

Religious zeal can harden into a heart that uses a sufferer as bait. Grace enables compassion; hearers remain responsible not to turn holy questions into weapons against love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew exposes motive: the question is framed “so that they might accuse him.” Orthodoxy without charity becomes courtroom strategy.

Apart from the Spirit’s softening, even Sabbath seriousness can prefer a charge over a cure. The Law’s Guardians miss the Law’s Giver standing before a broken man.

verses.text: He said to them, “What man is there among you who has one sheep, and if this one falls into a pit on the Sabbath day, won’t he grab on to it and lift it out?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus argues from their own practice. A sheep in a pit draws immediate rescue; no one waits for Monday. He appeals to conscience they already live by.

Classical Arminians treasure this humane reasoning: God enlightens through common sense and Scripture together, and people remain accountable for the mercy they already show animals. The gospel does not invent compassion; it recovers it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ binds them with a reductio they cannot escape. Their own Sabbath mercy toward livestock condemns their hardness toward a man.

The Son exposes inconsistency with authority. Revelation cuts through casuistry; the Lord who gave the Sabbath also names what love requires when life is in the pit.

verses.text: Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath day.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Human worth towers over livestock. Therefore “it is lawful to do good”—healing is not Sabbath violation but Sabbath-fitting mercy. The day serves life, not cruelty.

Wesleyans hear a wide summons to responsible goodness: grace frees and obliges believers to relieve suffering without fear of loveless fences. Doing good is not optional charity; it is aligned with God’s heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus states the a fortiori and then the verdict: good-doing is lawful on the Sabbath. The day’s holiness is not emptied; it is filled with mercy that reflects the Creator’s valuation of persons.

Christ interprets the Law from within. The Sabbath is reclaimed for the good God always intended—rest that does not abandon the needy, under the Lord who defines the day.

verses.text: Then he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out; and it was restored whole, just like the other.
verses.arminianNotes:
The command meets inability: a withered hand cannot stretch by nature. Yet Jesus speaks, the man acts, and restoration follows—healthy like the other. Word and response stand together.

Arminian readers often see enabling grace in narrative form: the Lord’s call supplies what He requires, without erasing the man’s stretching. Faith-shaped obedience is summoned and assisted; the healing magnifies both Christ’s power and a human response.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Stretch out your hand” is an effective word. What the man could not do, he does under Christ’s command, and the hand is restored. Sovereign power and human action are not rivals here.

The very Lord who creates life by speech restores the withered. The man’s stretching is not in doubt, yet it is fruit of the Savior’s effectual word—grace that heals, not mere advice waiting on unaided strength.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess Christ’s power and the man’s stretching. Arminians typically describe the command as grace that enables a free, assisted response; Calvin’s heirs generally describe it as Christ’s effectual word that restores and draws forth the act it commands.

verses.text: But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how they might destroy him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Mercy answered with a murder plot. Seeing good done, they leave to conspire destruction. Hardness of heart is not a small theological footnote; it is tragic, responsible refusal of light.

Arminians warn that grace resisted can deepen into hostility. The scene urges examination: will we celebrate Christ’s compassion, or cling to a righteousness that would rather silence Him than repent?
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew closes the unit with conspiracy. The Sabbath’s Lord has done good; His opponents plan to destroy Him. Evil is unmasked by its hatred of mercy.

The cross is already foreshadowed. Yet the plot cannot overturn God’s purpose—the Son they seek to destroy is the One through whom salvation will be accomplished. Worship answers their conspiracy with trust in the Christ they reject.
